qs.q: Which of the following best characterizes the airflow limitation seen in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)?
o: Completely reversible following treatment with inhaled short-acting beta-agonists
Persistent and not fully reversible, with progressive airflow limitation over time
Present only during acute viral infections and resolves entirely between episodes
Fixed airway obstruction that responds normally and fully to salbutamol
qs.e: COPD is defined by persistent airflow limitation that is not fully reversible, though it may improve slightly with salbutamol. Fully reversible airflow limitation is more characteristic of asthma rather than COPD.

qs.q: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) has ABG results showing pH 7.28, PaCO2 58 mmHg, and HCO3- 26 mEq/L. What is the primary acid-base disorder?
qs.e: The low pH (acidosis) and elevated PaCO2 (respiratory component, normal 35-45 mmHg) indicate a primary respiratory acidosis. The HCO3- is within the normal range, suggesting minimal or no renal compensation yet, pointing to an acute or acutely worsening respiratory acidosis.

qs.q: A 62-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease develops cor pulmonale with right ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the adaptive change in the right ventricle?
qs.e: Cardiac myocytes are permanent cells that cannot divide. Hypertrophy results from increased workload (pressure overload from pulmonary hypertension) causing increased synthesis of myofilaments and enlargement of existing cells, not an increase in cell number.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: COPD is a progressive airway disease causing irreversible airflow limitation due to chronic inflammation, airway remodeling, and loss of alveolar attachments. Diagnosis relies on spirometry and clinical context.

sections.p: COPD is defined by a post‑bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70 on spirometry, together with symptoms of dyspnoea, chronic cough or sputum production, and exposure to risk factors.
b: Symptoms must be chronic (≥3 months/year for >2 years)

t.b: Does the patient have irreversible airflow obstruction? A reduced FEV1/FVC confirms COPD; severity is graded by FEV1 % predicted.
Are there radiographic signs of hyperinflation or emphysema? May be normal; helps rule out other causes.

sections.p: The GOLD system stages COPD by post‑bronchodilator FEV1 % predicted and groups patients by symptom burden and exacerbation risk.

t.b: How symptomatic is the patient? Higher scores place the patient in GOLD groups B or D, guiding therapy intensity.
How many moderate/severe exacerbations in the past year? ≥2 or ≥1 leading to hospitalisation moves the patient to high‑risk groups.

sections.p: The dominant cause is chronic exposure to noxious particles, especially tobacco smoke. In low‑resource settings, biomass fuel smoke, occupational dust, and recurrent lower‑respiratory infections (TB, HIV‑related) are important contributors.

t.b: What is the primary irritant? Quantifies exposure and supports causality.
Are co‑existing infections accelerating airway damage? Positive tests prompt combined management.

sections.p: Patients develop progressive dyspnoea, chronic productive cough, and wheeze. Over time, barrel‑shaped chest, use of accessory muscles, and reduced exercise tolerance appear.
b: Chronic sputum production → suggests chronic bronchitis phenotype
Weight loss and pink‑puffer appearance → emphysema phenotype

sections.p: Beyond spirometry, tests identify comorbidities, infection, and severity.
b: Arterial blood gas if hypoxaemia suspected
Complete blood count to detect eosinophilia or infection

t.b: If unavailable, use pulse oximetry as a screening tool.
If culture not possible, treat empirically based on local resistance patterns.
Does the patient have predominant emphysema vs airway thickening? Helps tailor interventions and rule out alternative diagnoses.

sections.p: Acute exacerbations, respiratory failure, pneumothorax, pulmonary hypertension, and cor pulmonale are life‑threatening.
b: Sudden worsening dyspnoea with hypoxia → urgent care
Chest pain with unilateral breath sounds → suspect pneumothorax

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve symptoms, prevent exacerbations, and monitor disease progression.
b: Smoking cessation – the only intervention that slows decline
Bronchodilators (LABA/LAMA) – improve airflow and reduce symptoms
Inhaled corticosteroids – add for frequent exacerbations with eosinophilia

t.b: Why use LABA/LAMA? They relax airway smooth muscle, improve FEV1, and reduce exacerbations. Avoid monotherapy with short‑acting agents alone.
When indicated? In patients with ≥2 exacerbations/year and blood eosinophils ≥ 300 µL⁻¹. Avoid in low‑risk patients due to pneumonia risk.
When PaO2 < 55 mmHg or SaO2 < 88 % at rest? Long‑term oxygen improves survival; contraindicated if not meeting thresholds.

sections.p: Regular review of symptoms, inhaler technique, and spirometry every 1‑2 years; vaccinate annually; reinforce smoking cessation and physical activity.
Asthma, bronchiectasis, and interstitial lung disease can mimic COPD symptoms but differ in reversibility, imaging, and pathology.
b: Bronchiectasis – chronic sputum, dilated bronchi on CT

sections.p: Spirometry may appear normal in early disease; eosinophil count can be low despite steroid‑responsive phenotype; chest X‑ray often underestimates emphysema.
b: Normal FEV1/FVC in mild disease → consider repeat testing
Low eosinophils do not rule out benefit from inhaled steroids in frequent exacerbators

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe breathlessness or chest pain
Confusion or inability to speak full sentences

faq.q: Why does COPD cause a barrel chest?
faq.a: Chronic hyperinflation flattens the diaphragm and expands the rib cage, giving a barrel shape.
Airflow limitation is largely irreversible, but quitting smoking and optimal therapy can halt further decline.
When the patient has frequent exacerbations and elevated blood eosinophils, indicating an inflammatory phenotype.
